summary: This benchmark evaluates mechanistic activation editing and sparse attention routing in Qwen2.5-14B on a held-out Python class attribute completion task. It demonstrates that opening direct declaration-to-readout attention edges across just eight calibrated blocks accounts for 347 of 359 unrestricted reversals, whereas depth-matched controls account for zero. The methodology is statistically sound and rigorously controlled, though hardware details are sparse and scope is restricted to a single synthetic benchmark.
strengths: Rigorous experimental design featuring prespecified depth bins and strict depth-matched negative controls (the weaker 8 blocks).
Comprehensive ablation and baseline comparisons, including unrestricted all-blocks access, closed throughout, and leave-out evaluations.
Robust statistical reporting with paired bootstrap 95% confidence intervals and verified unedited clean baseline preservation.
Detailed reproducibility tracking of exact software dependencies, library versions (Python 3.12, MLX 0.32.4, NumPy 2.5.5), and pinned model commit hash.
weaknesses: Hardware specifications are insufficiently documented, referencing only an unspecified 'Studio run' without exact device model, chip variant, or unified memory configuration.
Narrow benchmark scope confined to a synthetic two-class attribute completion test in Python on a single model checkpoint.
The article is relatively terse and relies heavily on external links for detailed task schemas and implementation code rather than integrating qualitative examples into the text.
suggestions: Explicitly specify the complete hardware setup (e.g., Apple Mac Studio chip tier like M2/M3 Max/Ultra and unified memory capacity).
Provide a concrete prompt/completion example in the main text to illustrate the synthetic Python attribute query structure.
Test whether the identified eight attention blocks exhibit similar functional concentration on other identifier-binding tasks or natural language reference tasks.

claims.text: Only the first declaration receives the edit, after block 10 of frozen Qwen2.5-14B base revision 97e1e76335b7017d8f67c08a19d103c0504298c9.
We reuse the hidden-state displacement scores for blocks 18–48 from the earlier 64-group calibration.
The Studio run took eight minutes and 27 seconds using Python 3.12, MLX 0.32.4, MLX-LM 0.32.2 and NumPy 2.5.5.
